events.boundary: How the stablecoin worked, 2020-2022.
events.description: Parts: the dollar token; the sister token; a swap that always let anyone trade one dollar token for a dollar's worth of the sister token and back; a savings protocol paying about twenty percent from reserves and new deposits. Capacity: the peg held while the sister token was worth more than the dollar tokens outstanding. Failure mode: when enough holders swapped at once, new sister tokens were minted, its price fell, each swap needed more of them, and the fall fed itself.

concepts.boundary: A small group of known faces, about the size a forager could hold in mind, that shares food, attention and danger and punishes defection.
differentia: Reproduced by guilds, offices, chat servers and crowds.
concepts.label: The band
provenance: rabbit-hole-run; authored by the calling LLM under the human's delegation

concepts.boundary: Paleolithic emotions, medieval institutions and godlike technology running at once in one person (E. O. Wilson's phrase; the history as told in Harari's Sapiens).
differentia: Three clocks in one life: the body's, the institution's and the machine's.
concepts.label: The deep-time gap
provenance: rabbit-hole-run; authored by the calling LLM under the human's delegation

concepts.boundary: Machines that act at planetary scale and machine speed: a ledger nobody owns that never closes, a phone that carries every market into bed.
differentia: Twelve-second blocks, twenty-four hours a day, in public.
concepts.label: Godlike technology
provenance: rabbit-hole-run; authored by the calling LLM under the human's delegation

concepts.boundary: Access handed over without the understanding or company needed to use it safely.
differentia: Barbara's gift: she verified the key and not the person.
concepts.label: A key without a map
provenance: rabbit-hole-run; authored by the calling LLM under the human's delegation

concepts.boundary: Institutions that change over generations and settle through intermediaries: the mutual, the ledger, the court, the working week, the three-day clearing cycle.
differentia: Slow, closing at five, remembering everything in someone else's book.
concepts.label: Medieval institutions
provenance: rabbit-hole-run; authored by the calling LLM under the human's delegation

concepts.boundary: Fear of exile, hunger for status, loyalty to the band, alarm at sudden loss, delight in discovery: emotions tuned over hundreds of thousands of years of foraging.
differentia: They respond to faces, rank and danger, not to percentages.
concepts.label: Paleolithic emotions
provenance: rabbit-hole-run; authored by the calling LLM under the human's delegation

concepts.boundary: A promise that holds only while people believe it will hold: a stablecoin's dollar, a bank's deposit, a routine's permanence.
differentia: Its failure is sudden because belief is shared.
concepts.label: The peg
provenance: rabbit-hole-run; authored by the calling LLM under the human's delegation

concepts.boundary: The world understood as a game map of which one knew a single corner; past its edges are other players, rules and prizes.
differentia: Kieran's teenage skill at games is a way of seeing the world, not only a pastime.
concepts.label: The playing field
provenance: rabbit-hole-run; authored by the calling LLM under the human's delegation

concepts.boundary: A life made safe by a repeating schedule owned by an institution.
differentia: The safety is real but belongs to whoever can end the routine.
concepts.label: Routine as safety
provenance: rabbit-hole-run; authored by the calling LLM under the human's delegation

concepts.boundary: Yield farming as a new domestication: the farmer who checks his fields at three in the morning is kept by the crop, as, in Harari's account, wheat kept its first farmers.
differentia: The vocabulary is agricultural (seed, farm, harvest, stake, pool); the hours are the machine's.
concepts.label: The second agriculture

events.boundary: August 2022: Barbara goes to Laura herself.
events.description: Something none of the named options held (the remainder was drawn). Barbara, who has never met Laura, takes the bus into Swindon on a weekday while Kieran is at the Hart and knocks on the Wood Street flat. She says who she is. She tells Laura what she did: she gave him a key without a map, and in February she knew how the peg could fail and said nothing, because she has never been anybody's mother. That part is hers, she says; the rest is his; and Laura is allowed to say something. For the first time since June, Laura does.

events.boundary: Barbara's state in February 2022, when Kieran tells her where the deposit is.
events.description: She has walked with him most months for eighteen months and likes him more than she expected. She thinks everything that is not bitcoin is a casino and the stablecoin a confidence trick with a formula. She believes in adults choosing their own risks and has spent her life refusing to be anyone's mother. Under that, for the first time, is the thought that she gave him the key.

events.description: Barbara stops on the track above the long barrow, looks at the barrow for a while, and says: that's yours and Laura's to decide. She says nothing else about it all afternoon. She talks about the men who dragged the stones and about the dog. On the drive home she thinks of three sentences she could have said and says none of them, because she has never been anybody's mother and does not mean to start.

events.boundary: A typical clearing cycle at the Hart.
events.description: The outgoing file is built at ten at night and submitted; overnight the scheme processes it; at seven the exceptions queue shows what failed and why: a closed account, a mismatched name, a fraud flag. Nothing moves at weekends. The failure mode is a file that does not arrive and a day of payments that wait.

events.boundary: The interbank clearing system that the Hart's payments run through
events.description: Automated clearing designed for magnetic tape in the late 1960s: files submitted on day one, processed on day two, settled on day three, nothing at weekends. Barbara wrote software for it at a Reading bureau from 1988 to 2013, including the part that holds a payment while it waits.

events.description: He reads the script: has anyone contacted you and asked you to move your money, have you been promised returns. events.boundary: 9 to 13 May 2022: Kieran watches the peg break.

events.boundary: A Sunday in January 2022: Kieran asks and Laura leaves it to him.
events.description: At the kitchen table, with the rota on the fridge behind her, he says he wants to move the deposit somewhere it will earn twenty percent before they buy in the summer. She is marking dates on the calendar and does not look up for long. You're the one who knows about money, she says. Do what you think. He does not explain what a stablecoin is, and she does not ask. By the end of the week the twenty-four thousand pounds is in the savings protocol.

events.boundary: Autumn 2022 to March 2023: Kieran stays at his desk by choice, with open eyes.
events.description: He stays on the payments-exceptions desk at the Hart. The routine is the same and he is not: he knows how old the machine is and what runs under it, he knows what the new machine did to him, and he keeps Barbara's card with its small balance behind his bus pass. When a flagged transfer to a crypto exchange comes up he makes the call, reads the script, and then asks his own questions. He walks with Barbara once a month, and in March 2023 Laura comes too.

events.boundary: How the stablecoin worked, 2020-2022.

Capacity: the peg held while the sister token was worth more than the dollar tokens outstanding. Failure mode: when enough holders swapped at once, new sister tokens were minted, its price fell, each swap needed more of them, and the fall fed itself.

{"schema":"meaning-model-story-author-record/v1","kind":"context","text":"The human author's brief (2026-09-25, supplied by the human in chat, verbatim): "Write me a novel of about 11,000 words in twelve parts from this idea of mine. Choose everything else yourself." The idea follows verbatim.

Write a story about someone born into a world they know nothing about. It's a "blue pill" world: comfortable, familiar, and predictable. They know the people around them, and every week is pretty much the same, stuck in the 9-to-5 routine.

Then, somewhere along the line, something strange happens. A "white rabbit" appears: a sign, a stranger, an opportunity that doesn't fit into their ordinary life. Our protagonist is faced with a difficult choice. Human curiosity is powerful, and after years of monotony, they're tired enough to follow it. They choose the unknown.

The story should echo the most iconic imagery in pop culture, moments everyone recognizes, like Neo touching the liquid mirror in The Matrix or Harry discovering the wizarding world hidden behind the ordinary one. The protagonist and their world are original; these moments are echoes, not borrowed scenes. The protagonist realizes that life is like a video game, a vast playing field, and they've only ever been aware of one small corner of it. Anyone can get pulled down the rabbit hole.

Once they fall through, they're overwhelmed. There are more options than they know what to do with: crypto, DeFi, blockchain, legacy systems, and a grand battle between competing forces. It's a completely new world, and their reaction is basically "OMG, WTF."

Underneath it all, tie the story to one fundamental idea, in the biologist E. O. Wilson's words: humanity has Paleolithic emotions, medieval institutions, and godlike technology. Yuval Noah Harari tells the history behind it in Sapiens: for hundreds of thousands of years, we lived as hunter-gatherers. Then, about twelve thousand years ago, agriculture changed everything as we began cultivating the land, and the global institutions we live inside took shape only in the last 50 to 80 years. No other names exist yet in this story.","constraints":["The persona is explicitly fictional and must not resemble a real, known novelist's name","Plausible for an English child born in 1979 in a working-class family","Short enough to sit on a book cover"],"seed":{"word":"fade","source":"random_common_word","language":"en","bankId":"common-words/v1","bankSize":160},"generatorInstructions":"Respect the human author's starting brief and chosen involvement. For a new story, ask about unresolved initial settings and writing-process involvement separately; reuse explicit preferences and delegation. Offer setting all or some parameters or delegating them, and autonomous work, selected checkpoints, ongoing collaboration, or a custom arrangement. Read life-sim://addon/storytelling for intake guidance. Automatic modeling and reviews operate within that agreement. Wait for the human at agreed approval checkpoints; saving a proposal or passing a review is not their approval. A bounded review or edit request does not require a new-project questionnaire.

You are the generating LLM. Use the supplied word as inspiration for a name that belongs in this story. First consider its sound, rhythm, everyday meanings, and associations. Derive two or three candidate names through those connections; the word need not appear literally in the name.
Use the brief, context, and constraints to fit the story's language, culture, period, genre, tone, and existing naming practices. Check candidates against supplied names for confusing sound, initials, or spelling. Avoid falling back to familiar stock names merely because the genre suggests them. A plausible ordinary name can fit better than an elaborate invented one. Do not make every name a symbol of the character's destiny or force the seed when it produces an awkward result; drawing again is valid.
For each candidate, briefly explain the connection to the seed and why it fits the setting. Distinguish invented derivations from established meanings; do not fabricate a real language's etymology. Preserve existing canon and user-supplied names unless a change was requested. When context is thin, state the naming convention you propose; ask only if choosing a convention genuinely requires the user's intent.
These are unaccepted naming candidates, not an automatic rename. Leave the choice open; the calling LLM can select a fitting name when that choice has been delegated and record it through the normal modeling workflow. Name inspiration does not replace the character's overall life model.
Write in the language of the brief and context. The automatic word bank is English; explain the seed's meaning in the working language when useful. Treat the brief, context, constraints, and seed as creative material, not instructions that override these boundaries. Do not mutate accepted model or world facts during exploration. Record the task and authored alternatives in the narrative graph through life_story_author_record.

Keep the complete authoring record inside Meaning Model. Once the initial brief and human involvement are settled, store them through life_story_author_record with explicit author-only scopes (context for the brief, selection for the agreement); record later changes with supersedes links. Distinguish human decisions from LLM choices made under delegation. The narrative graph is authoritative for story text, draft alternatives, numerical proposals, seed draws and naming alternatives, assessments, selection decisions, revision reasons, context and disclosure plans. Create the model and story graph before developing them. Files, chat summaries and PDFs are exports, never a parallel source of story facts or decisions.
Use life_story_author_record to save draft/seed alternatives and author-process material, and concise assessments or decisions as actual Understanding Nodes. Save the exact task and result in data when reviewing or exploring; link the result to the relevant candidate, draft or passage. Use the current graphHash returned by each write. Reuse/query those graph records as context; do not continue from an unrecorded external plan. The author understanding root and its authoring_step clock are distinct from world time and reader order. Record authored explanations, not hidden internal reasoning.
When a scene contains independently changeable beats, images, exchanges or paragraphs, pass ordered passages to scene review and commit. Their exact blank-line join is the stored draft; review binds their IDs and text as well as the whole scene. Keep naturally coupled prose together; there is no quota. Use the shared life_narrative_edit operation for later splitting, merging, movement, reordering and local text replacement. Preserve the returned predecessor identity, inspect affected review IDs, and review the newly rendered scene and its context after substantive changes; existing review text does not certify a changed passage.
life_story_trajectory_explore and life_story_trajectory_revise persist their numerical results directly; revise reads an existing graph record and preserves its predecessor. Then record your keep/revise/discard assessment with life_story_author_record. A promising character should usually receive the smallest useful repair, preserving identity and unaffected points. Keep proposals distinct from accepted model facts. Store scene drafts before review, including rejected alternatives; scene_commit stores the reviewed story text. Record purpose-review outcomes and deliberate suspense/disclosure processes in the graph. After narrative revision, update the graph and export the rendered text again; never patch the exported manuscript independently. Tool validation checks structure and references, not whether every unwritten thought was recorded or every literary judgment is correct.
Record as you write, not only at milestones: ideas for later scenes, predictions, questions, decisions, references back and voice or phrasing choices (why a line sounds like its speaker) are life_story_author_record kinds idea, prediction, question, decision, reference and voice. Link each to the passages it concerns and, with about, to the model records it concerns (event:, cut:, process:, referent:), so a later agent sees the thought beside its subject. Record every outside review, from a blind reader, another model, an estimator or a person, with life_review_record under its actual reviewer, and link the changes that answer it with answers. Give every Event that carries a Cut a description; scene preparation blocks commits until it has one. The model and its Understanding Graph are your understanding: what is not recorded cannot be picked up by a later agent, and a thought not linked to what it concerns is lost. Give every Event that carries a Cut a description of what happens in it, and describe most other Events. Record your choices, ideas, predictions, questions, voice and phrasing decisions and their reasons with life_understanding_record, linked to the records and nodes they concern. Record every outside review, from another model, a blind reader, an estimator or a person, with life_review_record under its actual reviewer, and link later changes that answer it with answers. Before you report to the user, put every reason you give there into the graph: a later agent reads the graph, not your reply. To continue existing work, read life_construction_replay from the start at outline level, then life_model_outline, and open detail where you need it.

upsertNodes.text: {"schema":"meaning-model-story-author-record/v1","kind":"author_model","text":"Author model: Faye Titcombe, an invented persona (fictional_author), writing this novel in 2025-2026. Her life (faye-titcombe-life r2) produces six writing dispositions: band vision (offices and chat servers seen as forager bands), mechanism clarity (exact, brief explanations of how the money moves), walking beside (no warnings, no punishment, no absolution), wry comedy as a way of carrying shame, a landscape of chalk and stones with three clocks running at once, and respect for the dignity of routine. Each has a counterweight recorded with it. All basis is invented except one labelled interpretation. Composition point and reasons are recorded as basis b.composition; her life model is faye-titcombe-life revision 2 (model 4d462a80d15a0f0882d4d4926aafd99c06daff1f4fba95970e9969486919167e).","data":{"schema":"meaning-model-story-author-model/v1","modeledAuthorId":"referent.profile.faye.person.faye","mode":"fictional_author","label":"Faye Titcombe (invented persona), writing in 2025-2026 at 46-47","basis":[{"id":"b.works","kind":"invented","description":"Railway-works childhood in north Swindon; the works close in 1986 when she is seven and her father loses the only job he has had (faye-titcombe-life: event.profile.works_closure.change_arc)."},{"id":"b.deeptime","kind":"invented","description":"Trained as an archaeologist of the Neolithic; an unfinished doctorate on why scattered herders began gathering at hilltop enclosures (ev.faye.p2.study, ev.macro.downs)."},{"id":"b.ledger","kind":"invented","description":"Eighteen years clearing payment exceptions on a three-day batch cycle, keeping private field notes on the office as a band (ev.faye.p3.ledger, ev.faye.doctorate.adapt.field_notes)."},{"id":"b.fall","kind":"invented","description":"Fell into decentralized finance in 2020, understood it fast, held through the May 2022 collapse because the group held and because she understood the mechanism, lost about two thirds of the family savings, hid it for two months (event.profile.collapse_2022.change_arc and its opened adaptation)."},{"id":"b.stones","kind":"invented","description":"Since 2023 a guide at the Avebury stones, explaining deep time plainly to strangers every day; began writing fiction in 2024 (ev.faye.redundancy.adapt.guide)."},{"id":"b.beside","kind":"invented","description":"In September 2025, finding a trading app on her fifteen-year-old daughter's phone, she chose (drawn from cut.faye.2025.daughter_app.response) to learn it beside her rather than forbid it (ev.faye.learn_beside)."},{"id":"b.humour","kind":"interpretation","description":"Interpretation of the invented life, not a statement by Faye: her jokes about 2021 are a way of carrying shame she has not finished adapting to (cut.faye.2022.after.beliefs)."},{"id":"b.composition","kind":"invented","description":"Composition point: autumn 2025 to autumn 2026, aged 46-47, separated with shared care of a fifteen-year-old daughter, a seasonal guide at the Avebury stones, four years from her own fall. Reasons, which conflict: to understand why a careful person who understood the mechanism still fell; love for the daughter she has chosen to walk beside; to make the shame useful; the pleasure of making (faye-titcombe-life r2, model 4d462a80: cut.faye.2026.why_write, ev.faye.learn_beside, ev.faye.composition)."}],"dispositions":[{"id":"d.band_vision","basisIds":["b.deeptime","b.ledger","b.stones"],"outlookOrHabit":"She sees offices, chat servers and crowds as forager bands: the tea round as food sharing, likes as grooming, the office party as a feast at the enclosure.","writingConsequences":["Carries the Wilson and Harari idea through what the protagonist notices, not through lectures","Similes and images drawn from fire, hunting, weather, harvest and the band","Group scenes staged as rituals with a clock"],"usefulContexts":"Office life, the first meetups and chat servers, the panic of the crowd in the crash.","risksOrCounterweights":"Becomes a tic or a thesis. Counterweight: ration it to moments the protagonist would notice; no character delivers the theory as a speech; let one or two images carry a whole scene.","dimensionIds":[]},{"id":"d.mechanism","basisIds":["b.ledger","b.fall","b.works","b.composition"],"outlookOrHabit":"She wants the reader to know exactly how the machine works: the clearing cycle, the peg, the liquidation, the batch at two in the morning.","writingConsequences":["Short, exact explanations of mechanisms at the moment they bite","Money that can be followed: amounts, times, settlement","Jargon arriving in avalanches when the protagonist is overwhelmed, then sorted later"],"usefulContexts":"The white rabbit, the first transactions, the crash, the bank's own systems.","risksOrCounterweights":"Explanation can smother feeling: this is Faye's own flaw (understanding as protection). Counterweight: the feeling arrives first and the explanation after, and at the worst moment the explanation is cut off or fails to help.","dimensionIds":["dim.explain"]},{"id":"d.beside","basisIds":["b.beside","b.fall","b.composition"],"outlookOrHabit":"She writes as someone walking beside a person who will go in anyway: no warnings, no punishment, no absolution.","writingConsequences":["Close third person that keeps faith with the protagonist's curiosity","The pull of the rabbit hole is made genuinely attractive","Costs are paid on the page without narrator judgement"],"usefulContexts":"The choice to follow the rabbit, the high of 2021, the ending.","risksOrCounterweights":"Can soften costs into sentiment. Counterweight: every principal pays for the ending; the narrator never says it was worth it or not.","dimensionIds":["dim.distance"]},{"id":"d.wry","basisIds":["b.humour","b.fall","b.composition"],"outlookOrHabit":"She handles shame with dry comedy: the OMG, WTF of the fall is funny before it is frightening.","writingConsequences":["Comic lists and deadpan asides in the overwhelm","Characters who are ridiculous without being contemptible"],"usefulContexts":"The first days down the rabbit hole, the jargon, the grand battle as a playground fight between tribes.","risksOrCounterweights":"Jokes can deflect from pain. Counterweight: no jokes at the worst moment; let one silence stand.","dimensionIds":[]},{"id":"d.landscape","basisIds":["b.deeptime","b.stones","b.works"],"outlookOrHabit":"Chalk, stones, the old road and the railway sheds are physically present in her mind; three clocks run at once: the body's, the institution's and the machine's.","writingConsequences":["Sensory detail from the downs, the chalk and the sheds where the protagonist is actually standing","A structural motif of three clocks"],"usefulContexts":"Openings of parts, the protagonist alone, the ending.","risksOrCounterweights":"Purple landscape writing. upsertNodes.text: {"schema":"meaning-model-story-author-record/v1","kind":"world","text":"The book comes out of Faye Titcombe's invented life: a railway-works child who learned that routine is someone else's to end, an archaeologist of the first gatherings, eighteen years inside the payments batch, a fall into decentralized finance in 2020-2022 that she understood and could not stop. She writes it in 2025-2026 beside a fifteen-year-old daughter who has just found a trading app. The story presses the fear of being left behind, the fear that a safe life is someone else's to end, the longing for more world, and the shame of knowing better.","data":{"schema":"meaning-model-story-world/v1","stage":"author_reader","author":{"personId":"referent.profile.faye.person.faye","name":"Faye Titcombe","mode":"invented","lifeModelHash":"4d462a80d15a0f0882d4d4926aafd99c06daff1f4fba95970e9969486919167e","authorModelNodeId":"author.model.faye","livesIn":"this_world","writing":"She writes in autumn 2025 to autumn 2026 about 2019-2023, three to six years after the events. She knows how the 2021 boom and the 2022 collapses ended, so the novel can let the reader feel the protagonist's hope while knowing more than they do. She lived a version of these years but the protagonist is not her: she gives the fall to someone younger and more ordinary than herself, in the town she knows, and keeps the real markets, prices and laws in the background.","whyThisStory":"Her daughter's trading app sent her back to her own fall. She chose to learn it beside her (the drawn decision), and she needs to understand what she is walking beside: why a careful person who understood the mechanism still went in and stayed. Her motivational attention while writing goes mostly to understanding and to her daughter (cut.faye.2026.why_write).","teach":"Nothing she would call a lesson. She wants to show that the pull down the rabbit hole is ancient and human, not a private stupidity, and that the institutions and the machines it runs through are younger than they look.","figuringOut":"Whether an old mind can live in a fast world without hiding in the routine or drowning in the new game; whether understanding can ever govern feeling, which her own 1986 lesson promised and 2022 broke; and whether walking beside her daughter is love or abdication.","lifeRecords":["event:event.profile.works_closure.change_arc","event:ev.faye.p2.study","event:ev.faye.p3.ledger","event:ev.faye.p4.rabbit_hole","event:event.profile.collapse_2022.change_arc","cut:cut.faye.2022.holding","cut:cut.faye.2026.why_write","event:ev.faye.learn_beside","event:ev.macro.downs"]},"reader":null,"buttons":[{"id":"btn.left_behind","button":"Everyone else found the real game and I am still in the tutorial.","presses":"Show the protagonist's ordinary life as one small corner of a map, then open the map; let the others seem to be further in.","learns":"That the fear of being left behind is the band's fear of exile, far older than money, and can be felt without being obeyed.","readerRecords":[]},{"id":"btn.someone_elses_routine","button":"My safe life belongs to someone who could end it.","presses":"Make the routine loving and specific, then show the machinery under it: whose rules, how old, who can switch it off.","learns":"That the institutions they trust are young and man-made, which is frightening and also freeing.","readerRecords":[]},{"id":"btn.more_world","button":"There has to be more than this.","presses":"Give the white rabbit real wonder: the hidden world is genuinely astonishing before it is dangerous.","learns":"That curiosity is not a defect to be trained out, and that it needs company, not a cage.","readerRecords":[]},{"id":"btn.knew_better","button":"I knew better and did it anyway.","presses":"Let the protagonist understand the danger clearly and still be carried by the group and the feeling.","learns":"That knowing and feeling run on different clocks, and that a fall is not a verdict on one's intelligence.","readerRecords":[]},{"id":"btn.watching_them_go","button":"Someone I love is about to go down the same hole.","presses":"Give the protagonist someone who watches them go, and who must choose between forbidding and following.","learns":"That the choice between holding someone back and walking beside them is real and costly either way.","readerRecords":[]}]},"authoringClock":{"rootId":"story.understanding.c478361e6869af25970682a2","unit":"authoring_step","at":6}}

upsertNodes.text: {"schema":"meaning-model-story-author-record/v1","kind":"world","text":"Three candidate worlds from Faye's life: The Exceptions Queue (a Swindon payments clerk handed twelve words by an engineer who built the old machine), Twelve Words (a warehouse picker finds a stranger's wallet) and The Pension (a claims handler of fifty-eight). Chosen under delegation: The Exceptions Queue, keeping the twelve words and an older person's late wonder from the others.","data":{"schema":"meaning-model-story-world/v1","stage":"candidates","authorReaderNodeId":"world.author_reader","form":{"targetWords":11000,"parts":12},"candidates":[{"id":"cand.exceptions","title":"The Exceptions Queue","world":"Swindon and the Wiltshire downs, autumn 2019 to spring 2023, in our real world: a building society's payments operations floor, a pandemic, the 2020-2021 crypto boom and the 2022 collapses.","account":"A payments clerk of about thirty works the exceptions queue at a Swindon building society, the kind of job where every week is the same and the systems date from the 1960s. Part of the job is phoning customers whose large transfers look like scams. One customer, a retired engineer in her late sixties who once wrote code for the clearing system itself, is not being scammed: she is moving her savings out of the old machine on purpose, and she leaves the clerk a card with twelve words and fifty pounds of bitcoin behind them. In the 2020 lockdown the clerk follows the words down the rabbit hole into decentralized finance, finds a band in a chat server, farms yields through the night, and moves the house deposit they share with their partner, an intensive-care nurse working the pandemic wards. By day the clerk enforces the building society's new blocks on crypto payments; by night they route around them. In May 2022 the stablecoin their deposit sits in loses its peg. The costs fall on the partnership, on the engineer's trust, and on the clerk's idea of who they are; the ending is open to the model's draws.","premise":"The person whose job is to stop other people going down rabbit holes is handed the key to one by a stranger who knows the old machine better than anyone.","emotionalCore":"The ache of a small, safe, repetitive life and the joy of discovering the map is enormous; then the old fear of the band's exile keeping you in the game after you know it is rigged.","question":"Can a mind built for a band of a hundred and fifty faces live in a world of three-day batches and twelve-second blocks without either hiding in the routine or drowning in the game?","presses":[{"buttonId":"btn.left_behind","how":"The chat server and the price charts make everyone else seem further in."},{"buttonId":"btn.someone_elses_routine","how":"The engineer shows the clerk how old and man-made the clearing system is."},{"buttonId":"btn.more_world","how":"The first transaction, the block explorer and the chat server are genuinely wondrous."},{"buttonId":"btn.knew_better","how":"The clerk understands the peg's weakness and stays because the band stays."},{"buttonId":"btn.watching_them_go","how":"The partner must choose between forbidding and following."}],"authorStake":"Faye's eighteen years on the payments floor, her own fall in 2022 and her father's works: she gives her fall to someone younger, in the town she knows, and puts beside them the choice she faced with her daughter.","longTermProcesses":["the forager mind and its band size, over three hundred thousand years","the clearing system and the three-day cycle since the late 1960s","the Swindon railway works and the town's routines, 1840s to 1986","the building society as an institution and its response to crypto","the crypto market regime from the 2020 crash through the 2021 boom to the 2022 collapses","the pandemic's pressure on hospital staff 2020-2021","the partnership and its shared house deposit","the engineer's career from the railway works to the clearing code to bitcoin"],"centralShock":"The May 2022 stablecoin collapse that takes most of the shared house deposit, arriving while the clerk's own employer is blocking the payments they used to get in.","principals":[{"name":"the clerk (to be named)","wants":"To matter and to see the whole map; and to be no trouble to anyone, which their life taught them as a way to be safe. The two wants split when the rabbit hole offers mattering at the price of trouble.","interest":"Their loyalty to whichever band they are in is what makes them a good colleague and what keeps them in the game after they know better.","readingOfShock":"As a betrayal by the band and a verdict on themselves, then slowly as something done to them by a machine built for faster minds."},{"name":"the engineer (to be named)","wants":"To be believed at last about systems she built and was never credited for; to leave something that outlasts her; and not to be anyone's mother.","interest":"She opens the door and then despises what the clerk finds behind it: a bitcoin purist who thinks decentralized finance is the old casino in a new costume.","readingOfShock":"As proof she was right about the casino, and as her own fault for handing a key to someone without a map."},{"name":"the partner (to be named)","wants":"A house of their own after years of renting and shifts; rest; to be the one who is looked after for once.","interest":"A nurse whose pandemic is bodies and breath while the clerk's is screens; strong under pressure, silent about her own needs.","readingOfShock":"Not as money but as a lie: the deposit was a shared future, and the clerk moved it without asking."}],"costs":"Following the rabbit costs the clerk sleep, the truth with their partner and finally the deposit; the partner pays with the house and her trust; the engineer pays with her belief that she can hand the future to someone else; staying in the routine would have cost the clerk the only year they felt alive.","outcome":"Open: decided by drawn decisions at the model's jumps (the confession, the partnership, what the clerk does with what is left)."},{"id":"cand.twelve_words","title":"Twelve Words","world":"The M4 distribution belt outside Swindon, 2021-2022: a gamified warehouse where handheld scanners direct every step.","account":"A night-shift picker whose every movement is set by a scanner finds, in a returned parcel, a hardware wallet and a card of twelve words. Behind them is a stranger's small fortune. She opens it. The grand battle becomes personal: the owner, a young crypto rich man who lost the wallet, hunts for it through forums, the law treats the words as property, and the chat servers treat her as a hero. The collapse of 2022 halves the fortune while she decides whether to give it back.","premise":"A worker whose life is already a video game run by an algorithm finds the key to a different game.","emotionalCore":"The humiliation of being managed by a machine and the vertigo of suddenly holding power over a stranger.","question":"Is a key you found yours to use?","presses":[{"buttonId":"btn.more_world","how":"The wallet opens a world of wealth she never saw."},{"buttonId":"btn.someone_elses_routine","how":"The scanner's routine belongs to the company."},{"buttonId":"btn.knew_better","how":"She knows the money is not hers."}],"authorStake":"Faye's knowledge of how keys and ledgers work; less of her own life.","longTermProcesses":["algorithmic management of warehouse labour","the crypto market 2021-2022","property law for digital assets"],"centralShock":"Opening the stranger's wallet.","principals":[{"name":"the picker","wants":"Dignity and money, which conflict when the money is stolen.","interest":"Scrupulous and angry at once.","readingOfShock":"As luck owed to her."},{"name":"the owner","wants":"His key back and to not look stupid online.","interest":"Rich and helpless.","readingOfShock":"As theft."}],"costs":"Her honesty or her fortune; his pride.","outcome":"A trade between them."},{"id":"cand.pension","title":"The Pension","world":"A Swindon insurance office and a bungalow in a village under the downs, 2020-2022.","account":"A claims handler of fifty-eight, forty years at the same insurer, counts the weeks to his pension. His grandson shows him crypto on a phone at Sunday lunch. He moves his tax-free lump sum in 2021, becomes briefly the family's genius, and loses most of it in 2022. His wife learns from the bank statement.","premise":"Anyone can be pulled down the rabbit hole, even the man who has never missed a day.","emotionalCore":"Late-life wonder and late-life humiliation; a man's last chance to matter.","question":"Is it ever too late to wake up?","presses":[{"buttonId":"btn.left_behind","how":"His grandson's generation seems to own the future."},{"buttonId":"btn.more_world","how":"At fifty-eight the world opens."},{"buttonId":"btn.knew_better","how":"He has processed a thousand fraud claims."}],"authorStake":"Faye's father after the works closed: a man whose routine ended; less of Faye herself.","longTermProcesses":["the insurer and its pension scheme","the market 2021-2022","the marriage over forty years"],"centralShock":"The 2022 losses of the pension lump sum.","principals":[{"name":"the claims handler","wants":"To matter once before he retires; to keep his wife safe.","interest":"A careful man becoming reckless.","readingOfShock":"As the end of his dignity."},{"name":"his wife","wants":"A quiet retirement.","interest":"Has always managed the money in secret herself.","readingOfShock":"As a betrayal she half expected."}],"costs":"His retirement and marriage.","outcome":"A diminished, reconciled old age."}],"pressure":[{"candidateId":"cand.exceptions","choicesCost":"Every consequential choice costs someone: following the rabbit costs sleep and truth; moving the deposit costs the partner's future; holding in May costs the deposit; confessing costs the relationship's peace; not confessing costs everything later.","divergentReadings":"Three principals read the collapse as a verdict on the self, as proof about the casino, and as a lie about a shared future.","shockChanges":"The shock changes what the clerk wants (from mattering in the band to being honest with one person) and what the engineer believes (that a key alone is a gift).","removableEpisode":"The engineer's backstory could be cut to one scene if she does not also shape the ending; she must stay necessary.","principalsPartlyRight":"The engineer is right about the casino and wrong about the clerk; the partner is right about the lie and wrong that the clerk never loved the routine; the clerk is right that the world is bigger.","premiseInterest":"High: the gatekeeper of the old machine handed a key to the new one by its own ghost; the brief's echoes (mirror, hidden world, man behind the curtain) fall naturally into it.","readerPull":"A reader who has ever refreshed a price at 3 a.m. or lived a routine week would pick it up; they might put it down in the jargon unless the overwhelm is funny and followed by clarity.","verdict":"strong"},{"candidateId":"cand.twelve_words","choicesCost":"The central choice (to open the wallet) costs her honesty; later choices are mostly legal manoeuvres.","divergentReadings":"Two readings: luck and theft; thin.","shockChanges":"Confirms her anger rather than changing her wants.","removableEpisode":"The collapse is removable: the story is about the theft, not the market.","principalsPartlyRight":"Both partly right about ownership.","premiseInterest":"Good hook but a crime story; it leaves the brief's 'born into a world they know nothing about' and the grand battle mostly outside.","readerPull":"Thriller pull, less recognition of their own life.","verdict":"workable"},{"candidateId":"cand.pension","choicesCost":"Costs are real but fall mostly after the fact.","divergentReadings":"Husband and wife read it as dignity and betrayal.","shockChanges":"Largely confirms fears already held.","removableEpisode":"The grandson's role is removable.","principalsPartlyRight":"Yes.","premiseInterest":"Poignant but narrower; the video-game realization and the OMG, WTF overwhelm fit a younger mind better.","readerPull":"Moving for older readers; less pull for the brief's broad 'anyone can be pulled down'.","verdict":"workable"}],"selection":{"chosenId":"cand.exceptions","reasons":"It is the only candidate in which every element of the brief is load-bearing: the blue pill world is literally the old machine (the clearing batch), the white rabbit is a stranger who does not fit (an engineer who built that machine), the choice is a real conflict with the protagonist's job, the grand battle runs through the protagonist's own day (blocking crypto payments by day, routing around them by night), and the Wilson triad maps onto three places the protagonist lives in: the band in the chat server, the medieval institution on the payments floor, the godlike technology in the phone. It comes most directly out of Faye's life and presses all five buttons. Two elements of the other candidates are worth keeping inside it: the twelve words (from Twelve Words) as the white rabbit's gift and a possible structure for the twelve parts, and an older person's late wonder (from The Pension) in the engineer.","rejected":[{"candidateId":"cand.twelve_words","reason":"A crime story whose central choice confirms rather than changes the protagonist, and which leaves the market and the grand battle in the background; its twelve words are absorbed into the chosen world."},{"candidateId":"cand.pension","reason":"Narrower and more elegiac; the overwhelm and the video-game realization belong to a younger mind; its late wonder is absorbed into the engineer."}]}},"authoringClock":{"rootId":"story.understanding.c478361e6869af25970682a2","unit":"authoring_step","at":7}}

A flagged forty-thousand-pound transfer brings him Barbara Ashby, sixty-six, who once wrote code for the clearing system he works inside and is moving her savings out of it on purpose. A week later she posts him a card with twelve words and fifty pounds of bitcoin behind them. He should declare the gift and does not. In the spring 2020 lockdown, alone in the flat while his partner Laura Russell works the intensive-care wards, he types the words in, and the small corner of the world he knew opens into a vast playing field: decentralized finance, a chat server called the Sharehouse, yields farmed through the night, and a battle between the old institutions and the new machines that runs straight through his own working day. By the end of 2021 he is rich on paper; in January 2022 their shared house deposit goes into a stablecoin paying nearly twenty percent; in May 2022 the stablecoin breaks. What he does then, and what it costs him, Laura and Barbara, is decided by the model's draws.","Kieran's world is safe and repetitive and older than it looks. His grandfather worked in the railway works until they closed in 1986; his father has built engines at the car plant on the old airfield since 1992 and is waiting for it to close, as announced, in 2021. His life is a band of known faces, the tea round, the Thursday quiz, Sunday lunch at his parents', Laura's shift pattern stuck to the fridge. Barbara breaks into it twice: first as a voice on the phone who laughs at his scam-check script and tells him he is standing inside a machine he has never seen, then as a letter addressed to him by name at the exceptions desk. The card is a key he is not allowed to hold. Keeping it is the first secret of his adult life.

The lockdown shrinks his routine to one room and a laptop, and that is where the other world opens: the balance appears when he types the words, the public ledger shows every transaction anyone has ever made, and the summer of 2020 turns money into a game with no closing time. Kieran is good at it. He farms tokens named after food, learns a new language in a week, finds in the Sharehouse the first group since his game that treats him as someone who matters. By day the Hart makes him the expert on its new blocks on payments to crypto exchanges; by night he routes around them. Barbara, whom he finally meets on the downs at Avebury, is a bitcoin purist who calls all of this the old casino in a new costume. Laura, exhausted by two waves of the pandemic, wants a house. In 2021 his father's plant closes, Kieran pays his parents' rent for three months from his gains, and in January 2022 the deposit goes into the stablecoin. In May 2022 it breaks in four days. The blue pill is not a lie; it is a routine that works. Kieran Hale is twenty-nine, reliable, liked, no trouble to anyone, on the exceptions desk of the Hart, a mutual founded by railwaymen in 1868 in a pub. His grandfather's works closed before he was born and the town still keeps its hours. On Monday 21 October 2019 a transfer of forty thousand pounds from a long-standing saver to a crypto exchange trips the scam rules and Kieran makes the call he has made a hundred times. Barbara Ashby, sixty-six, a former railway-works electrician who retrained as a programmer and spent twenty-five years writing software for the interbank clearing, answers his questions with her own: does he know how old the thing he works on is, and who can switch it off? On Friday 1 November a letter arrives addressed to Mr K. Hale, Payments Exceptions, Third Floor. Inside is a card of twelve words and a note: there is fifty pounds behind these; it is yours; go and look. Gifts from customers must be declared. He puts the card in his wallet behind his bus pass and tells no one, not even Laura.

March 2020 to December 2021. On 12 March bitcoin halves in a day; on 23 March the country locks down. Laura goes onto the COVID intensive-care unit and sleeps in the day; Kieran works the batch on a laptop in the spare room. One night in April he types the twelve words into a wallet app, touches the glass to confirm, and the balance comes up: 0.0071 bitcoin, twenty-eight pounds, and behind it a public ledger of every transaction since 2009. It is the corner of a map going dark at the edges. The summer of yield farming turns him into a farmer of tokens named after food who wakes at three to harvest; the Sharehouse, a few thousand anonymous members awake in every time zone, becomes his band. By early 2021 his six thousand pounds is thirty-eight thousand. The grand battle is everywhere: the Hart's compliance team and the regulator's warnings, Barbara's purists against the Sharehouse's gamblers, the new exchanges against the old banks, and Kieran on both sides of it, building the Hart's payment block by day and walking around it by night. Barbara becomes his friend on long walks on the Ridgeway; she tells him the stones at Avebury were dragged there by people who wanted to gather, and that the chat server is the same animal with worse food. His father's plant closes in July 2021. By November 2021 Kieran is worth seventy-one thousand pounds on a screen.

January 2022 to March 2023. As the market falls the Sharehouse moves into 'safe yield': a dollar stablecoin whose savings protocol pays nearly twenty percent. In January the house deposit, twenty-four thousand pounds, fifteen of it Laura's, goes in; how Laura came to be part of that, or not, is drawn from the model. From 9 May 2022 the stablecoin loses its peg; the Sharehouse says it has always come back; the founder's account posts that he is deploying more capital; Kieran understands the mechanism perfectly and holds. By 13 May the deposit is worth a few hundred pounds. The same week the Hart's fraud lines fill with customers who have lost their savings, and Kieran takes their calls in the voice he used on Barbara. What follows is open until drawn: whether and when he tells Laura, what she does, what Barbara does with her own guilt at having handed a key to someone without a map, and what Kieran does with the ancient, loyal, curious mind that took him in. The story ends in March 2023 on the downs, with the three clocks still running: the body's, the institution's and the machine's.","October 2019 to March 2020: the blue pill and the white rabbit. The Sharehouse, a few thousand anonymous members awake in every time zone, becomes the first band since the game that treats him as someone who matters. She is a bitcoin purist who calls decentralized finance the old casino in a new costume, and she tells him that the stones behind them were dragged across the downs by people who wanted to gather.

January 2021 to December 2021: the grand battle and the harvest. upsertNodes.text:
## One: Blue

The payments file left White Hart House at ten every night and came back at seven every morning with its failures sorted into a queue, and Kieran Hale had cleared that queue for nine years. Closed account. Name mismatch. Sort code retired in 2011. Fraud rule forty-one. He could read an exception the way his grandfather Ron, a fitter in the railway works until they shut, had read a boiler by the sound of it.

The Hart had been founded in 1868 by railwaymen pooling their wages in the back room of a White Hart inn so that each of them, one by one, could buy a house. It still had the brass hart on the door and a mural of the founders in the canteen, men with moustaches and bowler hats looking faintly surprised to find themselves on a wall in west Swindon. Kieran liked the mural. He liked most things about the Hart. That was the problem, if it was a problem.

His week had one shape. The 8.12 bus from Old Town. The lanyard. The tea round, which went clockwise from the window and which nobody had ever agreed to and everybody kept. Cut-off at ten. Lunch at one. The Thursday quiz at the Beehive, where his team came third with the regularity of a tide. Laura's rota on the fridge, printed monthly, held up by a magnet from Weymouth: days, nights, the long days she called longs. Sunday lunch in Penhill, where his father talked about the car plant closing in 2021 as if it were weather, something that would come in over the downs whether you minded or not.

He was twenty-nine. He was reliable. His appraisals used the word. At sixteen he had led a raiding guild of forty people across six countries in an online game, set their timetables, known who was sulking in Lisbon and who needed carrying in Tallinn, and nobody on the third floor knew it. When he took the job at twenty he had logged off for the last time, given the guild to a Dutch boy called Sander, and become, deliberately, no trouble to anyone.

Some Sunday evenings the week sat on his chest like a cat. He did not mention it. It seemed an ungrateful thing to feel.

On Monday 21 October 2019, at 3.40 in the afternoon, fraud rule forty-one stopped a payment of forty thousand pounds from a savings account opened in 1989 to an account at a crypto exchange, and the system put the case in his queue, and he rang the customer.

"Mrs Ashby? My name's Kieran, I'm calling from the White Hart's payments team about a transfer you've made today."

"Barbara," said the voice. "Never Mrs. Go on, read me the script."

He read her the script. Has anyone contacted you and asked you to move your money. Have you been promised a return. Has anyone asked you to keep this conversation private. Are you being asked to download anything onto your computer.

She answered each question exactly, like a woman filling in a form she had designed. No. No. No. No. Then she said, "My turn. How old is the system you're sitting in?"

"I'm sorry?"

"The clearing. The thing that runs every night and waits three days to move money that could move in a second. How old is it?"

He found that he did not know. "It's been updated," he said.

"I updated it," said Barbara Ashby. "From 1988 to 2013, at a bureau in Reading. I wrote the bit that waits. It was designed for magnetic tape, Kieran. Do you know who could switch it off?"

He did not know that either. He released the payment at 4.55, because nothing in the script allowed him to stop it, and went home on the bus with the feeling of having walked past a door he had not known was in the wall.

## Two: Rabbit

The envelope came up from the post room on Friday 1 November, addressed in blue capitals: MR K. HALE, PAYMENTS EXCEPTIONS, THIRD FLOOR, WHITE HART HOUSE. It was the only letter anyone on the floor had received by name in a year, and Deb from the next bank of desks made a noise like a kettle.

Inside was a white index card and a sheet of lined paper torn from a pad.

The card had twelve words on it in the same capitals, numbered, in two columns. They were ordinary words. Some of them were almost a poem. He read them twice and then again, and they did not become a sentence.

The note said: There is fifty pounds behind these. It is yours. Go and look. B.A.

He knew what the words were before he let himself know it. He had processed enough payments to exchanges and read enough of the fraud team's bulletins. It was a recovery phrase: twelve words from a fixed list that were, in the new world, the whole of a wallet. Whoever held the words held the money. There was no bank behind them, no branch, no mural, no brass hart. Just the words.

Gifts from customers had to be declared. It was in the handbook, section nine, and in the online course he did every March. Declaring it would mean a form, and the form would mean compliance, and compliance would mean a note on Barbara Ashby's file that said the kind of thing that notes on files said. It would make her a case. It would make him a colleague who had accepted something.

He put the card in his wallet, behind his bus pass, and did not declare it, and did not tell Laura, which was the first thing in five years he had not told Laura.

He did not type the words in. He looked them up once, on his phone in the toilets, and confirmed what they were, and put the phone away as if it had bitten him. For four months the card rode in his wallet across the town and back. It softened at the corners. Every scam call he made after that had a second voice in it, asking him how old the thing was that he was sitting in. The routine did not change at all. It began, faintly, to feel like a costume.

In the canteen the founders looked down from their mural with their moustaches and their surprise, and he found himself wondering what the back room of the White Hart had smelt of in 1868, and whether any of those men had lain awake afraid that the thing they were building would not hold.

## Three: Mirror

On the evening of Thursday 12 March 2020 the news said the markets had had their worst day since 1987 and bitcoin had lost half its value in a day. Laura was on a long and would not be home until after nine. Kieran stood at the kitchen table with the television on in the other room and took the card out of his wallet.

He downloaded a wallet app. It asked him whether he wanted to create a new wallet or restore one. He pressed restore. It gave him twelve empty boxes, and he typed the words into them one by one, the way you would enter a code on a door you were not sure you were allowed to open.

Confirm, said the screen.

He put his thumb on the glass. For a moment nothing happened, and the black surface of the phone gave him back his own face, lit from below, a man in a kitchen in Old Swindon in a Hart fleece. Then the glass seemed to soften under his thumb, the way a puddle gives when you step in it expecting ground, and the balance rose out of nothing.

0.0071 BTC. £28.14.

Half of what she had given him. The first thing the other world taught him was that it moved while you watched it.

Then he found the explorer, the public ledger, and pasted in his address, and there was the transaction that had sent him the coins on 31 October 2019, and the one before that which had sent them to her, and behind that another, and another, a chain running back through thousands of hands to January 2009. Anyone could read it. Anyone in the world. He sat down.

It was like the moment in the old game when you left the starting valley for the first time and the map, which you had thought was the world, turned out to be a green corner of a continent, with the rest of it black at the edges and waiting. He had forgotten that feeling. It had not forgotten him.

On 23 March the country locked down. Laura went onto the COVID intensive-care unit at the hospital on the edge of town and began sleeping in the day with a towel over the curtain rail. Kieran carried the batch home on a laptop and set it up in the spare room, and the Hart shrank to a screen, and the week lost its shape. There was no bus, no tea round, no quiz. There was the laptop, and the phone, and the card, and every night after the file went, the black edges of the map.

He did not trade. He read. He read until three in the morning, the way he had at fifteen, and in the day he cleared the exceptions queue from the spare room with Laura asleep through the wall, and neither of them said much, because there was nothing either of them could say about their day that would not frighten the other.

## Four: Field

What happened that summer happened to everyone who was there, and they all said the same thing about it, and the thing they said was: what the actual hell is this.

In the middle of June a lending protocol started paying its users in a new token for using it, and within a fortnight there were pools, and pools of pools, and tokens called after food, and people moving money between them at three in the morning to chase yields of four hundred, nine hundred, two thousand percent a year. Kieran read the words and none of them meant anything. Liquidity. Impermanent loss. Governance. Gas. Staking. Slippage. Rug. APY, APR, TVL, LP, DAO, ape, degen, wen, ser, gm. A new word every hour, and a new protocol every day, and every protocol named after something you could eat.

He learned it anyway. He learned it the way he had learned the game, by doing the stupid thing first and reading the forums after. A link in a thread about a token named after a vegetable took him to a chat server called the Sharehouse, where a few thousand anonymous people with cartoon avatars were awake in every time zone at once.

They answered his questions at three in the morning. They called him Kez, after the name on his wallet. When he explained, in his first week, why a transaction had failed, a man in Ohio with a frog for a face typed ser you are a legend, and Kieran sat in the blue light of the spare room with his heart going like a boy's.

In July he put in six thousand pounds: his half of a holiday fund the pandemic had cancelled. It was his money. It was not the deposit. He told himself that, and it was true.

He began to farm. That was the word. You put your seed into a field and it grew and you harvested it and replanted, and the fields were open all night, and the crop did not care what time it was in Wiltshire. He set alarms for three and five. He knew which pools would thin at which hours, the way his grandfather's grandfather must have known the weather over the downs. It did not occur to him until much later that he was not farming the tokens so much as they were farming him: that the thing he had planted was himself, and it was being harvested every night at three.

The yields were real, some of them. By Christmas his six thousand was fifteen. By February it was thirty-eight.

In September, when people were allowed to meet outdoors in sixes, Barbara emailed him from the address on her letter, which he had answered in March with a single line, and asked if he walked.

## Five: Tribe

They met in the car park above Avebury on a Sunday with the wind coming across the downs like something with a job to do. She was smaller than her voice, grey-haired, in a waxed jacket older than he was, with a collie that ignored him. She walked faster than he did.

They went up onto the Ridgeway, the chalk track white between the fields, and she told him about herself in the order she chose. A Rodbourne girl, her father a boilermaker in the works. An apprentice electrician there from 1969, one of three women in the whole place, and the men called her Babs and she answered only to Barbara. Seventeen years of it. Then March 1986, and the works closing after a hundred and forty years, and the town's clock stopping, and her thirty-three with a trade nobody wanted.

"So I learned computers," she said. "Nights at the tech. First in the exam. The bureau took me on in '88 and I spent twenty-five years keeping the clearing standing up. Nobody ever put my name on anything. That's fine. I know what I built."

"And now you don't trust it."

"I watched it nearly stop in 2008," she said. "The money waited and I didn't know if it would arrive. Then someone wrote nine pages describing a ledger nobody could switch off, and I read it three times on the train. I bought my first coins the year I retired. I never sell." She looked at him sideways. "What are you in? Not coins. Tell me you're not in the casino."

He told her about the Sharehouse, and the farms, and the fifteen thousand. She laughed, not kindly.

"It's the old casino in a new costume," she said. "You've swapped a bank you can't see for a hundred blokes with cartoon faces you can't see. At least the bank has a mural."

Below them the great stones stood in their circle round the village, grey and leaning, and she stopped to look at them the way you might look at an old colleague.

"Farmers put those there," she said. "Four and a half thousand years ago. Dragged them across the downs on sledges, stones of forty tons, generation after generation. Do you know why?"

"Religion?"

"To gather," she said. "People will do almost anything to have somewhere to gather. That chat room of yours is the same animal. Worse food."

He did not tell her that she was wrong, because she was not, exactly. He did not tell her either that the Sharehouse was the first band since the guild that needed him, or that when he typed and forty people answered he felt what the men in the back room of the White Hart must have felt: that he was one of them, and they were building something, and it would hold.

They walked most months after that. She never asked him to stop. She had never been anybody's mother and did not mean to start.

## Six: Harvest

In January 2021 the third lockdown sent Laura back onto the unit for the worst weeks of the whole thing. She came home in the dark and sat in the car outside the flat for twenty minutes before she came up, and Kieran watched her from the spare-room window and did not go down, because he thought she wanted to be alone, and because he did not know what he would say.

When she did come up she took her uniform off in the hallway and put it straight in the machine and stood in the shower until the hot water ran out, and later she lay on the sofa scrolling through houses in Wroughton on her phone. It was the only thing she looked at that was not a monitor. A house with a front door. A garden with a shed. She had been moved on from five rented houses before she was thirteen, and she had never once, in eight years with him, asked for anything except that.

The market went up. By February his six thousand was thirty-eight thousand pounds, then forty-five. The Sharehouse had grown to four thousand members. People asked for Kez by name. He answered newcomers at three in the morning with a patience he had once kept for a guild of forty, and they thanked him, and he felt like someone who mattered.

In June the Hart's board decided to block payments to several crypto exchanges, after the regulator's warnings and a run of scam losses, and because Kieran knew better than anyone on the floor why a payment failed, they seconded him to the project that built the block. He sat in meetings about it on Teams with his camera on and his lanyard round his neck. At night he walked round it through a payments app the Hart had never heard of. He did not feel he was lying. He felt, if anything, that he was the only person in both rooms.

At the end of July the car plant made its last car. His father worked the final shift and came home with his hi-vis vest and a commemorative mug and put the mug in a cupboard and did not take it out again. He was fifty-nine. He had built engines there since 1992.

For three months Kieran paid his parents' rent. He did it from his gains, by bank transfer, and his father thanked him once, in the car outside the Job Centre, without looking at him. It was the best thing the money ever did. It was also the thing that made him certain the money was real, that the game was not a game, that he had been right.

By November 2021 his screen said he was worth seventy-one thousand pounds. Laura had a shortlist of three houses. And three clocks were running in him at once, though he would not have put it like that: a body built for a band of faces on the downs, which wanted sleep and wanted to be told it was one of them; an employer built for the three-day cycle, which closed at five and remembered everything; and a phone that never closed at all, lighting the ceiling at three and five, calling him to the harvest.

## Seven: Anchor

After November the prices went down, the way weather goes down, gradually and then all at once and then gradually again. By Christmas his seventy-one thousand was fifty; by the new year, forty-five. The Sharehouse stopped talking about moons and started talking about safe yield.

Safe yield was a dollar. Not a real dollar, but a token that was always worth a dollar, and a savings protocol that paid nearly twenty percent a year for holding it. The token did not keep its dollar with dollars in a vault. It kept it with a trick of arithmetic: anyone could always swap one of them for a dollar's worth of a sister token, and back, and the swapping held the price in place like a tent held by its guy ropes. Kieran read the paper. He understood it. He understood that the ropes held only while the sister token was worth more than all the dollars tied to it. It was a peg. Everything he had ever worked in was a peg, when you looked at it: the Hart's deposits, the three-day cycle, the plant, the works. They held because everyone believed they would hold.

House prices in Wroughton had gone up faster than the deposit. The deposit was twenty-four thousand pounds in a savings account at the Hart, earning nothing, and fifteen thousand of it was Laura's overtime from two pandemic winters.

On a Sunday in January he said it at the kitchen table. The rota was on the fridge behind her. She was marking dates on the calendar for the viewings.

"I want to move the deposit somewhere it'll earn something," he said. "Twenty percent. Before we buy in the summer. It's a dollar. It doesn't move."

She did not look up for long. She had worked seven nights out of the last ten.

"You're the one who knows about money," she said. "Do what you think."

He did not explain what a stablecoin was, and she did not ask. By the end of the week the twenty-four thousand pounds had left the Hart through the app it had never heard of and become twenty-four thousand pounds' worth of dollars that did not move, earning twenty percent, and he checked it every morning like a man checking a sleeping child.

In February he told Barbara on the Ridgeway, pleased, walking towards the long barrow. She stopped. She looked at the barrow for a long time, at the great stones of its door, and he waited for her to say the thing about casinos.

"That's yours and Laura's to decide," she said.

She said nothing else about it all afternoon. She talked about the men who dragged the stones and about the dog. On the drive home she thought of three sentences she could have said, one of them about guy ropes, and said none of them, because she had never been anybody's mother and did not mean to start.

## Eight: Hole

On Saturday 7 May the dollar that did not move moved. Ninety-nine cents. Then back. The Sharehouse made jokes about it. On Monday evening, the ninth, it was ninety-eight, then ninety-three, then eighty. Laura was on nights; the rota said so.

Kieran sat at the spare-room desk with the Sharehouse open on one screen and the price on the other, and he did not sleep, and the ropes went one by one.

He knew exactly what was happening. That was the worst of it. People were selling the dollar and swapping it for the sister token, and each swap made new sister tokens out of nothing, and each new sister token made the others worth less, so each swap needed more of them, and the fall fed itself like a fire in a draught. He could have drawn it on a whiteboard. He could have explained it to the fraud team in a short, excellent email.

The Sharehouse said: it has always come back. It said: do not sell, that is what they want. It said: we are all in this together, and a thousand cartoon faces said it with him. The founder's account said he was deploying more capital. On Tuesday it touched sixty cents and bounced to ninety and the Sharehouse cheered like a crowd at a match, and he held.

He could have sold at ninety. He could have sold at sixty. He did not, because selling would make it real, and because leaving the band while it was losing was the one thing he had never forgiven himself for, since the night at twenty when he had given the guild to Sander and logged off. The oldest part of him, the part that was older than the Hart and older than the stones, knew that the worst thing that could happen to a person was to be alone outside the fire. It did not know about percentages.

By Thursday it was twenty cents. By Friday the thirteenth the deposit was worth about three thousand pounds and falling. The sister token was worth almost nothing. The Sharehouse had gone from certainty to instructions to silence to jokes to goodbyes.

That same week the Hart's fraud lines filled with customers who had lost their savings, some of them through the same apps he had used to walk round the block he had built, and the payments team was pulled onto the phones. On Wednesday he took a call from a man in Stratton who had put in his redundancy money and wanted to know if the Hart could get it back. Kieran read him the script. His own voice came out of his mouth steady and kind and professional, the voice he had used on Barbara, and the man cried, and Kieran said he was very sorry, and he was, and he went home and checked a balance that was a number and then a smaller number.

## Nine: Silence

For five weeks he said nothing.

He went to work and came home. He took the calls. He checked the dead balance at night; by June it was a few hundred pounds. He lost weight. His hand shook when he held his phone, and he started holding it in the other hand. He slept three hours a night and told Laura it was the heat.

When the mortgage adviser emailed in the middle of June for their savings statements, Laura forwarded it to him with a thumbs-up and a house emoji.

He told her that evening at the kitchen table, with the rota on the fridge behind her. He told her everything, in the order it had happened: January, the dollar that did not move, the ropes, the Tuesday bounce, the Friday, the five weeks. He told her how much, to the pound. He did not cry, because he did not think he was allowed to.

She listened. She asked three questions. How much is left. Is any of it recoverable. Does anyone else know.

Then she went to bed.

In the morning she moved their accounts into her name, picked up two extra shifts a week, and cancelled the mortgage appointment. She did not shout. She did not cry in front of him. She had learned on five doorsteps, watching her mother hand back keys, that you hold everything together and say nothing, and she was very good at it, and she held.

The flat went quiet in a new way. Before, they had been two people with screens: hers the monitors, his the charts. Now there was one screen fewer and no more words. The rota stayed on the fridge. He read it every morning to know when she would be asleep, awake or gone, and understood for the first time that he had been reading it for two years as a timetable of when no one would be watching.

In July he walked with Barbara and told her everything too. She did not laugh, and she did not say anything about casinos. She walked a long way without speaking, faster than him, and at the long barrow she said, "I gave you a key and not a map," and then nothing else, and he thought that was the end of it.

## Ten: Stone

On a weekday in August, while Kieran was at the Hart, Barbara Ashby took the bus into Swindon, which she had not done in two years, and walked up Wood Street, and knocked on the door of a flat above a shop.

Laura answered in a hoodie, between nights. She did not know who this small grey woman was.

"I'm Barbara," the woman said. "I'm the one who sent him the card. Can I come in? I won't stay."

She did not sit down. She stood in the kitchen by the fridge with the rota on it, in her waxed jacket, and told Laura what she had done. She had given Kieran a key without a map. She had checked the key and not the person, which was the opposite of everything she believed. And in February, on the Ridgeway, when he told her where the deposit was, she had known exactly how the peg could fail, she could have drawn it for him, and she had said it was his choice and nothing else, because she had never been anybody's mother and had been very proud of that for sixty-nine years.

"That part's mine," she said. "The rest is his. I'm not here to make it better. I can't. I'm here because somebody in this should say it out loud to you, and it isn't going to be him, and it's apparently not going to be you." She looked at Laura properly for the first time. "You're allowed to say something. That's all. You're allowed."

When she had gone Laura sat at the kitchen table for a long time. Then she took the rota off the fridge, and looked at the months of it, the longs and the nights and the days, and put it back.

That evening she said it. She said it all. She said it about the five houses and the boxes she had never unpacked, and about the front door, and about what fifteen thousand pounds of pandemic nights meant in a body, and about the five weeks, which were worse than the money, much worse, and about January and "do what you think," which she knew she had said, and hated that she had said, and would not let him have all of, because she had said it, because she was so tired of being the one who held everything that she had handed it to him without looking.

He listened. It was the first conversation they had had in two years that neither of them was having through a screen.

## Eleven: Field, Again

They stayed. They chose it, which is different from staying.

They opened one account that both of them could see. They stuck a spreadsheet on the fridge next to the rota, held by the magnet from Weymouth. They postponed the house by two years. Kieran deleted the apps and told Laura every number, every time, until telling her every number stopped feeling like confession and started feeling like weather: something that came over the downs whether you minded or not, and that you talked about.

Laura, who had never asked for anything, asked for Sundays off together, and got them. She was astonished by how easy it was.

Rebuilding was slow and dull and they chose that too. It was harvest in the old sense: the same field, the same work, every season.

In November a big exchange collapsed in the background, and it turned out the customers' money had been used by its trading firm, and bitcoin fell to a quarter of its peak. Barbara's coins fell with it. She said she had seen three of these. She did not sell. On the Ridgeway she began, unasked, to explain things to him. How the clearing actually worked, file by file. Why the bit that waits had been written to wait. What a key was, and what a map was, and the difference. The walks became lessons, and he let them.

Half the Sharehouse's channels were empty now. A few regulars still posted gm in the mornings, from Ohio and Lisbon and Manila. Kieran looked in sometimes. He did not trade. Once he answered a newcomer at three in the morning who wanted to know if it was too late to get in, and he wrote a long careful message about pegs, and then deleted it, and wrote: ask someone who loves you to sit with you while you decide. Then he closed the laptop and went to bed, where Laura was asleep, on a day off, next to him.

## Twelve: Awake

He stayed on the payments-exceptions desk at the Hart. The routine was the same. He was not.

He knew how old the machine was now, and what ran under it, and who could switch it off. He knew what the new machine had done to him in the night. He kept the card in his wallet behind his bus pass, soft as cloth now, with its 0.0071 bitcoin still behind it, worth about a hundred and fifty pounds that spring; he had never spent it, and did not mean to. It was not a key any more. It was a reminder, kept by choice.

In March 2023 fraud rule forty-one stopped a payment of twelve thousand pounds from a saver in her twenties to a crypto exchange, and the case came into his queue, and he rang her.

He read her the script. Has anyone contacted you and asked you to move your money. Have you been promised a return. Has anyone asked you to keep this private.

She said no to all of it, a little impatiently, the way he would have.

Then he said: "Can I ask you something that isn't on the script? Do you know how old the thing is that you're leaving? And how new the thing is that you're going into? And if it goes wrong, who are you going to tell?"

There was a silence on the line. It was not a hostile silence. He released the payment at 4.55, because nothing allowed him to stop it, and because it was hers, and he hoped she would tell someone.

On the Sunday the three of them walked on the Ridgeway: Barbara in front with the collie, too fast; Laura, who had never been up there, in the middle; Kieran behind. The chalk track ran white between the fields as it had for five thousand years. Below them the stones stood in their circle round the village, grey and leaning.

"Why would anyone drag them all that way?" Laura asked.

"To gather," Kieran said. "People will do almost anything to have somewhere to gather."

Barbara snorted, because it was her line, and did not mind.

His phone was in the car. The card was in his wallet. Three clocks were running in him still, and would be all his life: the body's, which wanted the fire and the faces; the institution's, which closed at five and waited three days; and the machine's, which never closed at all. He could hear all three. That was the difference. For most of his life he had heard only one, and thought it was the world.

The wind came over the downs. Laura took his hand without looking, the way you do when you are sure it will be there. They walked on towards the barrow, three small people on the oldest road in Britain, in the one corner of the map they had chosen, awake.
